# Phase 0: Breadth first — Stanford CS336

*weeks 1–2* · [Track on the site](https://arubad.github.io/AI_Research_Journey/#p0)

Watch all 17 lectures of [Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch](https://cs336.stanford.edu/spring2025/) ([YouTube playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLoROMvodv4rOY23Y0BoGoBGgQ1zmU_MT_)) before any deep dive. Alisa started her search this way; it gives the skeleton that organizes every scattered concept, and its five assignments are the best self-study implementation track that exists. Watch at 1.5x, take notes, draw one diagram per lecture. Do not pause to implement yet.

## Assignments
- [A1 Basics](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment1-basics) — HAND
- [A2 Systems](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment2-systems) — HAND→AGENT
- [A3 Scaling](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment3-scaling) — HAND→AGENT
- [A4 Data](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment4-data) — HAND→AGENT
- [A5 Alignment](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment5-alignment) — HAND→AGENT

**Assignment plan.** [A1 Basics](https://github.com/stanford-cs336/assignment1-basics) is HAND: tokenizer, model, optimizer, training loop, written with autocomplete off (the course itself asks for this). Alisa calls it crucial because implementing and debugging a Transformer comes up so often that it must become muscle memory. A2, A3, A4, A5 are HAND→AGENT: write the core (the online-softmax tile, the IsoFLOP fit, the dedup pass, the GRPO loss) yourself, let agents build the harnesses. Compute for self-study: a single H100 runs ~$2–3/hour on [RunPod](https://runpod.io/pricing) or [Lambda](https://lambda.ai/pricing); debug on CPU first.
